items.q: What two things does all software success depend on?
items.a: **Understanding** the system and **executing on that understanding**.

items.q: Which two understandings matter most for an engineer?
items.a: The system's **actual behavior**, and how to **change it correctly and safely**.

items.q: Why does hard-to-understand code get worse over time?
items.a: Each confusing change **raises future risk**, and the effect **compounds non-linearly**.

items.q: What four factors place software on the disposable–durable spectrum?
items.a: **Consequences of failure**, **cost of replacement**, **dependents** and **cost of maintenance**.

items.q: What's an example of disposable software?
items.a: A **one-off party planner** or a personal calculator: if it fails, **nobody cares**.

items.q: Is durable software going away with AI?
items.a: No: it stays the **most important** and grows too; **err on the side of durable**.

items.q: How can you make a system safely more disposable?
items.a: **Isolated environments**, **enforced independence**, a **durable fallback** and **limited scope**.

items.q: Why does standardization lower the cost of rigor?
items.a: It **removes possibilities**: one language, framework and protocol means less to check.
Checks that **just run** automatically, **fast and reliable**, with few false positives.

items.q: How can coding agents make testing cheaper?
items.a: By writing **in-memory fakes** of services so every test is **fast and deterministic**.

items.q: Why turn linter strictness to maximum early?
items.a: It **ends debates** and avoids a giant clean-up when you turn it on later.
